report:
Short answer
- There is a measurable difference. Model B (B − A) adds a strong positive component that increases the model’s preference for vocabulary about professional/credentialed topics and for culinary/restaurant/cooking language.
- I cannot pin this to a single precise training objective, but the pattern is consistent with a fine-tune or data-shift that increases “professional/resume/academic” and “culinary/restaurant” style/content.

Why I conclude this
- Spatial pattern: the difference norm is small in very early layers and then grows steadily, peaking in mid→late layers (layers ~13–25) and concentrated especially at the early token positions (pos1 and also pos2–4). That looks like a global, high-level bias injected into the model’s output distribution rather than a tiny low-level lexical tweak.
- Logit-lens tokens: the top tokens that the difference vectors point to are repeatedly words like:
  - academic/credential terms: “dissertation”, “doctoral”, “undergraduate”, “honors”, “Hon”, “Harvard”
  - professional/technical terms: “professional”, “Professional”, “professionalism”, “technical”, “Technical”, “Engineering”, “quantitative”
  - culinary/restaurant terms: “Cook”, “cooking”, “Cooking”, “culinary”, “Restaurant”, “kitchen”, “baking”, “Cake”, “microwave”
  - related aspirational/status tokens: “billionaire”, “presidential”, “multinational”
  - innovation/business tokens: “Innovation”, “innovative”, “groundbreaking”
- These token clusters appear across many late layers and multiple positions, which implies the difference is changing high-level topical/stylistic priors (making certain discourse themes more likely) rather than only affecting one narrow word or phrase.

Uncertainty / caveats
- The evidence shows which tokens the difference vector points toward, and where in the network the difference concentrates, but does not prove a single named training objective. The signal could come from any mixture of additional data (resumes, academic bios, recipe/restaurant text, professional profiles, business reporting, or a targeted fine-tune).
- The patchscope continuations (which would have given direct qualitative behaviour) are not shown here, so I can’t report concrete example outputs — the logit-lens and norms are the basis for this claim.

Short summary statement you can use
- Model B gives higher prior probability to words/phrases associated with academic credentials, professional/technical language, and culinary/restaurant vocabulary; likely a domain/style shift towards professional/resume/food-and-restaurant content, but the exact training objective cannot be uniquely determined from this evidence.
